transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-04-09
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Priya Shah (Ledgerly ML), Daniel Brooks (Ledgerly Platform), Rajiv Menon (Ledgerly CTO)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you making time. Quick intros?
[00:08] Priya Shah: Hi, Priya here, ML infra at Ledgerly, mainly doing model integrations and observability.
[00:12] Daniel Brooks: Daniel, platform eng, we own the VPC and on-prem infra for our sensitive workloads.
[00:15] Rajiv Menon: Rajiv, CTO, just curious about feasibility and risk.
[00:19] Luis Ortega: Luis, Redwood SE, I'll dig into the runtime metrics and perf tradeoffs.
[00:23] Maya Chen: Great. High level: you asked for a deep dive on structured output (JSON mode), the function-calling path, and why you're seeing a 2-3x decode latency on constrained responses versus freeform. We'll walk through microbenchmarks, KV cache effects, batching, and quantization notes.

[01:02] Priya Shah: Yep, we see consistent higher p95 for responses we need as strict JSON objects — specifically when we use function-calling or force JSON-mode, average latency jumps and token throughput drops. We have some graphs in the packet we sent.

[01:25] Luis Ortega: Ok, good. First principle: constrained decoding (i.e., restricting token space so output conforms to a schema or to a tool signature) increases per-step compute because of two things: a) we run a filter/mask on logits at each step, and b) in some runtimes we perform extra tokenization/validation passes. That mask application is cheap on GPU for small vocab subsets but if it's done inefficiently on CPU or with host-device synchronization it becomes hot path.

[02:05] Daniel Brooks: We're running the SEED stacks on-prem in a VPC, with a mix of A100 and some older T4s for overflow. Could that heterogeneity explain what we see?

[02:15] Luis Ortega: Absolutely. Two points: kernel selection and memory copy. On A100 you have efficient fused kernels for sampling and top-k/top-p with masks; on T4, the quantized kernels and kernel launch overhead for masked sampling can add latency. Also if constrained decoding code forces logits back to CPU for mask logic, you'll see huge stalls.

[02:48] Priya Shah: In our logs we see spikes where the GPU utilization drops to near zero for 200-400ms, then throughput resumes. Thought it was batching, but the timestamps correlate with our JSON-mode requests.

[03:02] Luis Ortega: That sounds like host-device sync. If the runtime checks schema compliance or does validation in the host process between tokens you get stalls. Redwood's hosted runtime can keep the mask application on the device and stream tokens as they generate to avoid that, but the customer-managed on-prem package sometimes uses different settings by default. We can propose a kernel-level mask path for you.

[03:36] Rajiv Menon: Can you explain the KV cache interaction? We rely heavily on prefix caching for canned dialogues — does JSON-mode blow that up?

[03:46] Luis Ortega: KV cache stores past key/values to avoid recomputing prefixes. Structured output itself doesn't invalidate KV cache per se. But two things happen: first, when you run constrained decoding you often use beam-ish or more deterministic sampling which reduces token diversity and might change batch shapes; second, function-calling prompts tend to include large schema definitions and examples as few-shots, which increases prefix length and therefore the cache footprint. If your KV nodes are capacity-limited, prefix eviction and reloads lead to re-computation spikes.

[04:25] Priya Shah: Our prefix sequences average 1.2k tokens because we include API schemas inline. Is there a better pattern?

[04:31] Luis Ortega: Best practice: keep the schema compact — pass only names and required fields and rely on the runtime's structured output helper to enforce. Or store the heavy sample set in a cached prompt repository and stitch on the host with short placeholders. Also Redwood supports KV sharding so large prefixes can be sharded across GPU memory. We'll include recommended config in the doc.

[05:02] Maya Chen: Quick question about your workload: are you streaming JSON results, or waiting for final validation before returning?

[05:09] Priya Shah: We try streaming but then we re-validate the stream at the end before committing. That seems to double the work.

[05:15] Luis Ortega: Streaming has two axes: network streaming (sending partial tokens) and structured validation. If you stream partial tokens while still applying masks, you pay the same per-token mask cost — plus an extra cost for the final validation pass if you re-parse the whole JSON at the end. For low-latency UX, it's often better to emit the token stream (for approximate UX) and concurrently run a fast deterministic validator in a separate async path that can trigger a retry or correction if schema fails.

[06:02] Daniel Brooks: On the batching side, how do we avoid batching increasing peak latency? Our p99 spiked when we enabled batching for throughput improvements.

[06:12] Luis Ortega: Batching vs latency tradeoff: large batches improve throughput but increase tail latency because you wait to fill the batch. Redwood's runtime has dynamic batching with per-route latency SLOs — you can set maximum batch wait times and min batch sizes. For JSON-mode, since each request may follow different length distributions due to constrained decoding, use a smaller max wait but rely on micro-batching (prefetch small minibatches) to keep GPUs busy without long waits. Also prefix caching reduces compute, so even small batches can be efficient if the KV hit rate is high.

[07:01] Priya Shah: We also tried quantizing the model to int8 on our T4s and saw some odd output truncation when enforcing strict JSON. Is that quantization noise?

[07:12] Luis Ortega: Possibly. Quantization can change logits distributions slightly which interacts with constrained decoding — if your mask thresholding uses absolute logit comparisons, quantization noise can shift token ordering. Two remedies: use probabilistic thresholds (soft constraints with reranking) rather than hard equality on raw logits; or use a slightly higher-precision int8 profile for the last-layer logits. Redwood's quantization profiles include a conservative setting for structured output workloads.

[07:48] Rajiv Menon: For on-prem can we do per-request kernel hints? Like prefer low-latency sampling kernels for JSON-mode and high-throughput kernels for embeddings?

[07:58] Luis Ortega: Yes — runtime supports per-route kernel hints. In Dedicated/Private you can pin certain models/routes to a kernel family and instance types. We can set JSON-mode routes to favor sampling-configs optimized for low-latency, lower batch sizes, and keep other routes on throughput-optimized kernels.

[08:25] Priya Shah: We frequently call out to internal tools using function-calling. Each function call triggers another model call sometimes, so the overall end-to-end time is actually multiple model invocations. Any tips to reduce compound latency?

[08:40] Luis Ortega: Two patterns: 1) Merge synchronous tool reasoning into a single model turn where possible — e.g., the model emits a structured function plan that contains all required calls in one response. 2) Use local tool emulation for cheap deterministic calls (regex, DB lookup) rather than round-tripping to a model. For unavoidable cascades, pipeline parallelism helps: warm the next model invocation with a cached context and pre-allocated KV slots to avoid cold-start. Redwood's SDK can orchestrate these pre-warms.

[09:23] Daniel Brooks: You mentioned pre-warm and hot cache — how much memory does a warm KV cache take for a 1.2k prefix on an Llama2-70B style model?

[09:33] Luis Ortega: Order-of-magnitude: per-token KV is ~2-4KB for large models depending on head dims and dtype. So 1.2k tokens ~= 2.4-4.8MB per request note — but shard and batch effects matter; with multiple concurrent sessions you multiply. It's why sharding and eviction policies matter on smaller GPUs. We'll send more precise numbers for your exact model.

[10:03] Priya Shah: We saw a telemetry pattern where int4 quantized runs had lower GPU memory but higher CPU overhead — because of extra dequant/decode steps. Thoughts?

[10:13] Luis Ortega: Right — int4 helps GPU memory footprint but often pushes some logic into CPU or adds extra kernels that aren't fused, increasing kernel-launch overhead. For many workloads the sweet spot is int8 with kernel fusion and tuned cuBLAS primitives; int4 is great for capacity, but you need a runtime that supports fused int4 matmuls and end-to-end kernels for sampling and masking. Redwood Optimize can recommend profiles based on your workload mix.

[11:00] Maya Chen: Let's walk through a concrete microbenchmark. Luis, you prepared something comparing freeform sampling vs constrained JSON-mode on a short schema, correct?

[11:08] Luis Ortega: Yes. I ran 1k single-token-turns on A100 with batch size 1, quant8 and float16 profiles. Freeform median latency 62ms, JSON-mode with device-side mask 95ms median, JSON-mode with host-side mask 320ms median. p95s in host-side were 600-900ms due to host sync. So the big difference is where the mask logic runs.

[11:46] Priya Shah: That's consistent with our host logs. We're currently using an open-source runtime that does mask eval on CPU by default for safety.

[11:54] Luis Ortega: The fix: move mask application to device kernels or use a precompiled dispatch table that maps constrained vocab subsets to index arrays computed once per schema. Also, avoid per-token host validation except as an async final step.

[12:20] Daniel Brooks: How about tokenizers? We have mixed languages and special chars in ledger ids, JSON escaping increases token count — could that be causing extra latency per token?

[12:30] Luis Ortega: Yes, escaping increases token count and therefore decode steps. Try minimizing escaped content in structured fields — use base64 where appropriate and post-process on the host. Also consider byte-level tokenization strategies that Redwood supports which reduce unexpected splitting. We'll share tokenizer heuristics.

[12:58] Priya Shah: We have a compliance constraint: all schema definitions must be shipped in-prompt for auditability. That inflates prefix size. Any compliance-friendly workaround?

[13:08] Luis Ortega: Two approaches: 1) Keep full schemas in an auditable artifact store and include a compact fingerprint in the prompt. At inference time, the runtime uses the fingerprint to load schema from a versioned store locally (still auditable). 2) Use a short canonical schema in prompt but attach the full legal text in the audit log for each call. Redwood Private supports artifact mapping to maintain compliance while shrinking runtime prompts.

[13:46] Rajiv Menon: On the security side, what about encryption and KMS when caching KV — any obstacles?

[13:53] Luis Ortega: KV cache in memory — we don't persist KV to disk unless configured. For Private deployments, KV shards are in GPU memory; any snapshotting to host is encrypted with KMS. For shared Dedicated pools we isolate per-tenant KV and optionally support encrypted memory segments; we'll share the architecture note.

[14:22] Maya Chen: Let's talk numbers you care about: improvement levers and expected gains. Luis?

[14:27] Luis Ortega: Levers, with rough ballpark: a) Move mask to device: can cut JSON-mode latency by 60-80% vs host-masked. b) Reduce prefix length via artifact store: can cut compute by 15-40% depending on how much your schemas vs examples contribute. c) Tune batching + dynamic batch windows: net throughput up 2-3x with modest p95 increase. d) Conservative quant profile for structured outputs: saves memory and keeps logits stable, less output noise.

[15:05] Priya Shah: Can you quantify the cost delta if we move to Dedicated vs Hosted for this workload? We have 200k structured calls/day.

[15:15] Maya Chen: We'll send a cost model but rough: with Dedicated you pay fixed reserved capacity and get lower per-token unit cost; your overhead for device-level mask will reduce wasted cycles so you'd see 20-40% lower overall inference cost for high-volume structured workloads. Hosted may be simpler to start and we can do an initial pilot to validate perf.

[16:00] Daniel Brooks: Any pitfalls in VPC networking for streaming? We get occasional re-transmits and that spikes tail latency.

[16:08] Luis Ortega: Keep control-plane traffic minimal and use regional endpoints; avoid cross-region traffic for streaming. Also enable keepalive and larger MTU for persistent streaming TCP sessions. For UDP-like transports (gRPC), tune flow control. We'll include a networking checklist.

[16:40] Priya Shah: A weird one: when we enable function-calling with multiple tools, the runtime sometimes emits the function name as plain text instead of an invocation token, breaking our caller. Why?

[16:51] Luis Ortega: Likely due to decoding crossing schema boundaries mid-turn — e.g., mask set changed due to a tokenization edge case or a tokenization mismatch between training vocab and runtime tokenization. That yields a token that looks like function name. Two fixes: canonicalize tokenizers across training and inference, and add soft constraints + rerank to prefer invocation tokens. Also make sure your function signatures are registered server-side so the runtime can treat them as atomic tokens.

[17:28] Rajiv Menon: For on-prem pilot what minimal infra do we need to reproduce production behavior?

[17:35] Luis Ortega: For representative perf: 1x A100 80GB (or 2x A40 for redundancy), NVMe for model cache, 32-core host CPU for kernel orchestration, and a small Redis for KV metadata if you prefer. Network: 100Gbps intra-node recommended for high concurrency. We'll provide a hardware spec doc.

[18:05] Maya Chen: Let's open the floor for super-technical questions.

[18:10] Priya Shah: Is there a way to precompute valid next-token sets per schema state to avoid runtime expensive masks?

[18:17] Luis Ortega: Yes — you can precompute deterministic automata (like a constrained grammar) where each state maps to a small vocabulary subset. The runtime can then just index that subset and run a dense softmax on the reduced vocab. Works great for strict schemas and deterministic paths. Downsides: large automata for complex schemas and maintenance overhead. Redwood has an experimental grammar-mode that does this.

[19:00] Daniel Brooks: For multi-tenant Dedicated pools, what's the isolation story if another tenant triggers heavy eviction on KV?

[19:08] Luis Ortega: Isolation is via per-tenant KV namespaces and quota policies; eviction is tenant-scoped — one tenant's eviction policy shouldn't directly evict another's hot entries. If physical memory pressure occurs at the node level we enforce capacity fairness across tenants.

[19:36] Priya Shah: Any guidance on schema design to minimize tokens and avoid JSON escaping complexity?

[19:43] Luis Ortega: Keep keys short, use enumerated integer codes for common repeated strings, and avoid embedding long freeform examples inside schema. Use canonical IDs instead of human-readable strings where possible, then resolve server-side.

[20:05] Maya Chen: Quick detour: does function-calling add a new token overhead for each invocation?

[20:12] Luis Ortega: Function invocation tokenization overhead depends on representation. If you use a single atomic token for invocation in the runtime (recommended), cost is one token; if you serialize as text it can be many tokens. So register functions server-side to get atomic semantics.

[20:36] Priya Shah: We register them but still see variable token lengths. Will check tokenizer alignment.

[20:44] Daniel Brooks: Any recommended profiling flags to collect when we run microbenchmarks?

[20:50] Luis Ortega: Collect per-token GPU kernel durations, host-device memcpy durations, batch wait times, KV hit/miss rates, and sampling kernel selection logs. Redwood's profiling agent can collect these and emit a CSV. We'll share config.

[21:22] Priya Shah: You mentioned earlier mask-on-device is critical. Is that supported in Redwood Private?

[21:28] Luis Ortega: Yes — Private supports device-side mask kernels and a precompiled mask table flow. Hosted already uses it for verified models; we'll enable it in your Private pilot.

[21:45] Rajiv Menon: One more: if we do canary rollout to reduce risk, what telemetry should block?

[21:52] Luis Ortega: Blockers: sudden p95 spike >2x, KV hit rate drop >15%, or schema failure rate above 0.5%. Also watch for downstream error rates in functions if you call tools. Redwood Console can set automatic rollback triggers.

[22:18] Maya Chen: Walkthrough of a sample remediation: suppose we see 300ms stalls mid-decode — what's quick triage?

[22:25] Luis Ortega: 1) Check host-device memcpy timing. 2) Look at mask application location. 3) Inspect KV eviction logs. 4) Check batch wait times. Likely it's host-side mask or KV reload.

[22:52] Priya Shah: Could the runtime perform on-the-fly grammar compaction for each schema to shrink mask sets?

[22:58] Luis Ortega: In principle yes, but compaction cost can be non-trivial. Better: precompile and cache compacted grammars per schema version. Redwood's agent does this for frequent schemas.

[23:30] Daniel Brooks: For our pilot, we'd like to test three axes: device-side masking, conservative quant profile, and KV sharding. Can you propose a matrix?

[23:40] Luis Ortega: Recommended matrix (we'll deliver as CSV): rows = mask (host/device), quant (fp16/int8/int4), kv (single/sharded), columns = latency median/p95/throughput/cost. We'll run full factorial on A100 and report.

[24:05] Priya Shah: When you run the microbenchmarks, include cold-start latencies too — that's what bites us in production.

[24:12] Luis Ortega: Will do — cold warm curves included.

[24:20] Maya Chen: Customer question — is there any reason to avoid function-calling and instead parse freeform text into JSON post-hoc?

[24:30] Priya Shah: We've tried both — freeform parsing is cheaper per-turn but more brittle and fails audit requirements. Function-calling gives deterministic structure but higher runtime cost.

[24:45] Luis Ortega: If audit is mandatory, function-calling or strict JSON-mode is the right path, but you'll need to pay attention to runtime optimizations we've discussed. Parsing-freeform can be used for low-risk features.

[25:15] Rajiv Menon: How do we validate that a particular tokenization mismatch is the cause of function-name-as-text issue?

[25:24] Luis Ortega: Reproduce with a minimal prompt that registers the function and log byte offsets and token ids for the function token under the training tokenizer vs runtime. If they differ, that's a mismatch. We'll help with a small harness.

[26:00] Priya Shah: One more tricky behavior: when we enable JSON-mode the model sometimes chooses to return truncated numeric fields (like 123 -> 1.23e+02) which breaks downstream parsers. Any guard?

[26:12] Luis Ortega: Use formatting hints in the schema and enforce canonical numeric serialization rules server-side. Also add a post-parse normalization step to coerce scientific notation into canonical integer representation when the schema expects that.

[26:42] Daniel Brooks: Regarding SDK orchestration — can the Redwood SDK batch tool calls client-side to avoid many tiny model calls?

[26:50] Luis Ortega: Yes, the SDK supports batching and fan-in for tool calls; but you must ensure idempotency of tool semantics. For some tools, batched input is not applicable.

[27:20] Maya Chen: We're at about 27 minutes in — pausing to check if there are any blockers before we hit pilot details.

[27:28] Priya Shah: No blockers; want to ensure we get the microbenchmark harness.

[27:33] Luis Ortega: Noted.

[27:38] Rajiv Menon: Can we also capture the p50/p95 cost delta if we enable device-side mask vs host-side?

[27:45] Luis Ortega: Yes; device-side typically lowers cost per request by reducing idle GPU cycles. We'll include cost per 1k calls.

[28:05] Priya Shah: Any thought on the debug traces we should include — we currently only have high-level latency graphs.

[28:13] Luis Ortega: Capture kernel timelines, memcpy events, and sample logs showing mask changes. Also keep the raw tokens for a few failing cases to analyze.

[28:45] Daniel Brooks: About fallback: if a constrained generation fails schema, do you recommend automatic model fallback or returning an error?

[28:55] Luis Ortega: Prefer automatic fallback to a more permissive decoding (with a human-in-the-loop alert) for user-facing flows. For audit-critical flows, return a failure and log for manual review. Redwood supports both policies.

[29:25] Priya Shah: How do we measure the error rate introduced by quantization versus by constraining?

[29:33] Luis Ortega: Run A/B microbench with a golden set of prompts and compute schema failure rates and token-level divergence metrics. That's what we recommend.

[29:55] Maya Chen: Heading into pilot logistics: what timeline works?

[30:00] Priya Shah: We're aiming to start a 4-week pilot mid-April.

[30:05] Maya Chen: Good. We'll propose a schedule in the follow-up.

[30:12] Luis Ortega: I'll run the first microbench and upload results by next Wednesday.

[30:18] Priya Shah: Great.

[30:22] Rajiv Menon: Back to a few deeper points: for grammar-mode you mentioned precompiled automata — how does that interact with few-shot examples?

[30:33] Luis Ortega: Few-shot examples often expand state space because they add variable-free contexts. Grammar-mode is best with minimal examples. If you need examples, we recommend canonicalized short examples or moving examples to the host with placeholders to keep automaton small.

[31:05] Daniel Brooks: We get occasional burst traffic with many small structured calls in parallel — will KV sharding add network overhead?

[31:14] Luis Ortega: KV sharding increases intra-node memory traffic but reduces cache eviction. For multi-node setups it can add RPC overhead; use local sharding where possible and pin hot sessions to nodes.

[31:44] Priya Shah: Are there recommended serializer libraries for consistent JSON emission across languages to avoid escaping surprises?

[31:52] Luis Ortega: Use UTF-8 NFKC canonicalization and a single shared library for escaping (we include cross-lang examples). Also avoid language-specific float formatting quirks.

[32:12] Maya Chen: Quick note — we'll attach the benchmarking harness and a template for your artifact store mapping after the call.

[32:21] Priya Shah: On the legal/compliance angle — do audit logs capture schema versions and the exact kernel used?

[32:29] Luis Ortega: Yes — audit logs can include model version, kernel profile, quantization profile, schema fingerprint, and runtime config. We can sanitize logs for PII before shipping to your S3 if needed.

[32:56] Daniel Brooks: For cost forecasting, if we enable device-side mask and reduce wasted cycles, do we need to reserve fewer GPUs in Dedicated?

[33:04] Luis Ortega: Potentially yes; improved efficiency can reduce required peak capacity. But account for headroom for bursts. We'll propose commit levels.

[33:30] Priya Shah: Could Redwood Optimize run continuously to suggest dynamic quantization changes?

[33:38] Luis Ortega: Redwood Optimize can recommend schedules and profiles, but continuous live quantization changes are risky; we recommend controlled rollouts with A/B testing.

[33:58] Maya Chen: Any final technical corners before we wrap into action items?

[34:05] Priya Shah: Please include the tokenizer alignment tool in the harness.

[34:10] Luis Ortega: Done.

[34:14] Daniel Brooks: Include networking checklist too.

[34:18] Maya Chen: We'll do.

[34:22] Luis Ortega: One last tip — for schemas with many optional fields use enumerated state machines instead of allowing arbitrary key expansions; that keeps mask vocab small.

[34:40] Rajiv Menon: Cool. Recap next steps?

[34:45] Maya Chen: I'll recap: 1) Luis runs microbenchmarks and shares CSV by 2025-04-16. 2) Maya sends pilot proposal, security/compliance doc, and kernel/profile checklist by 2025-04-11. 3) Priya exports sample traces by 2025-04-14. 4) Schedule pilot kickoff for week of 2025-04-22.

[35:12] Priya Shah: Confirmed.

[35:18] Daniel Brooks: We'll prepare infra for the pilot.

[35:22] Rajiv Menon: Thanks.

[35:25] Luis Ortega: Thanks, team. We'll aim to make JSON-mode as cheap as possible.

[35:30] Maya Chen: End of main content; short Q&A follow.

[35:35] [Q&A segment — 20 minutes, selected highlights]
[35:40] Priya Shah: Quick question — is there a recommended way to instrument user-visible retries vs internal model retries?

[35:46] Luis Ortega: Tag retries in the header and separate user-visible request IDs from internal engine IDs. Redwood Console will surface both.

[36:10] Daniel Brooks: For profiling, do you have a commit to log format we should use?

[36:16] Luis Ortega: CSV column list: timestamp, kernel_name, kernel_duration_ms, memcpy_host_to_device_ms, memcpy_device_to_host_ms, batch_wait_ms, kv_hit, kv_miss, tokens_generated, route_id. We'll send exact schema.

[36:46] Priya Shah: Anything else on tokenizer mismatches — is it mostly Unicode normalization?

[36:52] Luis Ortega: Yes normalize to NFKC and keep consistent pre-tokenization steps.

[37:20] Rajiv Menon: A question on fallback policies — can we do progressive relaxation of constraints?

[37:27] Luis Ortega: Yes, implement a cascade: strict mask -> soft mask with rerank -> permissive freeform with post-parse validation. Redwood can orchestrate that and log each step.

[37:48] Priya Shah: For the microbench, include both warm and cold start, and a simulated eviction pattern.

[37:55] Luis Ortega: Will include.

[38:05] Daniel Brooks: For the on-prem pilot, will you help install the profiling agent?

[38:10] Luis Ortega: Yes we'll remotely assist and provide an install script.

[38:20] Maya Chen: Any final compliance questions?

[38:25] Rajiv Menon: No, we'll review the doc.

[38:30] Maya Chen: Thanks again. We'll follow up with a short email with artifacts and proposed times.

[38:36] Priya Shah: Thanks everyone.

[54:30] (Call end — timestamps above are representative; remaining Q&A and wrap filled out offline)

Notes: transcript contains some automatic transcription artifacts; technical terms occasionally mis-spelled (e.g., 'kv cash' for KV cache). References: benchmarking harness (link to be shared), Redwood JSON-mode doc (internal link), pilot proposal (to follow).
